options.text: `const a`, because `ReactNode` only accepts React elements, never plain strings
options.why: `ReactNode` is the broad type: strings, numbers, null, booleans, arrays and elements all fit.

options.text: `const b`, because `null` is not a valid value for a required `children` prop
options.why: `null` is part of `ReactNode`, so passing it to `Panel` type-checks.

options.text: `const c`, because `ReactElement` accepts elements only, so a text child fails
options.why: TypeScript reports that `Card` doesn't accept text as child elements.

options.text:
`const d`, because `

` creates an intrinsic element rather than a `ReactElement`
options.why:
An intrinsic element such as `

` is still a `ReactElement`, so `d` compiles.

explanation: Use `ReactNode` for `children` when anything renderable is allowed, which is almost always. `ReactElement` means exactly one element object (what JSX produces), so text, numbers and `null` are rejected: `<Card>Hello</Card>` fails with "components don't accept text as child elements". Reach for `ReactElement` only when you really need an element, for example to clone it. Verified with TypeScript 6 and @types/react 19.

options.text: `Event`, the DOM event type that React passes straight to its handlers
options.why: React passes its own `ChangeEvent` wrapper, which isn't assignable from a DOM `Event` parameter here.

options.text: `ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>`, so `e.target` is the input element
options.why: The generic fixes the target type, and `value` exists on `HTMLInputElement`.

options.text: `ChangeEvent<HTMLElement>`, the widest element type that covers any input
options.why: `HTMLElement` has no `value` property, so `e.target.value` is a compile error.

options.text: `FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>`, since an input change bubbles to its form
options.why: The handler is on the input, so its event type is a change event targeting the input.

explanation: Inline handlers get their type from context, but a handler declared separately needs an annotation, or `strict` reports an implicit `any`. React's synthetic events are generic over the element: `ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>` gives `e.target.value: string`. `ChangeEvent<HTMLElement>` fails because a plain `HTMLElement` has no `value`, and a DOM `Event` parameter isn't compatible with React's `ChangeEventHandler`. Verified with TypeScript 6 and @types/react 19.

options.text: Add `import type { T } from 'react'` so the compiler recognises the name
options.why: `T` is a type parameter, not an import; the problem is the parser reading `<T>` as JSX.

options.text: Rename the file to `.ts`, since generics are not allowed in `.tsx` files
options.why: Generics are allowed in `.tsx`; a `.ts` file couldn't contain the JSX at all.

options.text: Write the type parameter as `<T,>` so it isn't parsed as a JSX tag
options.why: The trailing comma or a constraint tells the parser this is a type parameter list.

options.text: Move `<T>` after the parameter list: `(props: …)<T> => …`
options.why: That isn't valid syntax: type parameters must come before the parameter list.

explanation: In `.tsx` files, `<T>(…) =>` is ambiguous: it looks like the start of a JSX element. Writing `<T,>` or `<T extends unknown>` makes it unambiguously a type parameter list. A `function List<T>(…)` declaration avoids the issue entirely. Verified with TypeScript 6: the plain `<T>` form produced TS17008, and `<T,>` compiled cleanly.

stem: In React 19, setting `Greeting.propTypes = { name: PropTypes.string }` on a function component still logs a development warning when you render `<Greeting name={42} />`.

options.text: True
options.why: React 19 removed propTypes checking, so nothing is logged even in development.

options.text: False
options.why: React 19 silently ignores `propTypes`; use TypeScript or runtime validation instead.

explanation:
React 19 removed `propTypes` checks (and `defaultProps` for function components). The property is ignored without any warning, so code that relied on it gets no checking at all. The React team recommends TypeScript for compile-time checks, plus a runtime validator such as Zod at data boundaries. Verified with React 19.3 in development: `` rendered `

Hi 42

` and logged no errors.
reference: React 19 upgrade guide: Removed propTypes and defaultProps

options.text: Install `@types/jsx`, which now ships the JSX namespace separately
options.why: There is no such package; the namespace moved under the `React` export.

options.text: Use `React.JSX.Element`, or drop the annotation and let TypeScript infer it
options.why: React 19 types removed the global `JSX` namespace in favour of `React.JSX`.

options.text: Set `"jsx": "preserve"` in tsconfig so the compiler declares JSX globally again
options.why: The `jsx` option controls emit, not whether a global namespace exists.

options.text: Change the return type to `HTMLElement`, which is what a component returns
options.why: Components return React nodes, not DOM elements; `HTMLElement` is the wrong type.

explanation: React 19's types removed the global `JSX` namespace, so `JSX.Element` no longer resolves. Use `React.JSX.Element` (`import type { JSX } from 'react'` also works), or simply omit the return annotation, since TypeScript infers it. The official codemod `types-react-codemod` rewrites these references. Verified with TypeScript 6 and @types/react 19.3 (error TS2503).

options.text: `useState` can't hold objects; store `id` and `name` in two separate states
options.why: State can hold any value, including objects; the problem is the inferred type.

options.text: The initial `null` makes the type `null`; use `useState<User | null>(null)`
options.why: With no type argument, TypeScript infers `null` and rejects any object later.

options.text: `setUser` needs a callback here: `setUser(() => ({ id: 1, name: 'Ann' }))`
options.why: An updater function still has to return the state type, which is still `null`.

options.text: Objects must be frozen first: `setUser(Object.freeze({ id: 1, name: 'Ann' }))`
options.why: Freezing doesn't change the type; the state type is still `null`.

explanation: `useState` infers its type from the initial value. `useState(null)` gives a state of type `null`, so `setUser({...})` fails ("'name' does not exist in type '(prevState: null) => null'"). Provide the type explicitly, as in `useState<User | null>(null)`, then narrow with `user?.name` or an `if (user)` check when reading. Verified with TypeScript 6 and @types/react 19.

options.text: Both lines compile, because a ref's `current` is typed `any` until React attaches it
options.why: Ref types are precise; neither line compiles under React 19's types.

options.text: Only the `focus()` call fails: `useRef<number>()` still creates a mutable ref without an argument
options.why: React 19 types made the initial argument required, so `useRef<number>()` fails too.

options.text: `inputRef.current` may be `null`, and `useRef<number>()` fails for lack of an initial value
options.why: Use `inputRef.current?.focus()` and `useRef<number | undefined>(undefined)`.

options.text: Only `useRef<number>()` fails; `inputRef.current` is non-null inside an effect
options.why: TypeScript doesn't know about commit timing, so `current` stays `HTMLInputElement | null`.

explanation: With React 19's types, `useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)` returns `RefObject<HTMLInputElement | null>`. Even inside an effect TypeScript reports "'inputRef.current' is possibly 'null'", so write `inputRef.current?.focus()`. React 19 also made the argument to `useRef` required ("Expected 1 arguments, but got 0"), so write `useRef<number | undefined>(undefined)`. All refs are now mutable `RefObject`s; the old read-only `MutableRefObject` split is gone. Verified with TypeScript 6 and @types/react 19.3.
reference: React 19 upgrade guide: useRef requires an argument

options.text: Version 1 is right; the error means `TextField` must also forward `ref` explicitly
options.why: The error comes from the props type itself, not from refs.

options.text: Native `size` is a `number`, so the whole props type becomes `never`; version 2 omits it
options.why: Intersecting `number` with `'sm' | 'lg'` is empty, so `Omit` the native prop first.

options.text: `ComponentProps` only works with components, so `ComponentProps<'input'>` resolves to `{}`
options.why: `ComponentProps<'input'>` resolves to the full set of native input props.

options.text: Both versions are equivalent; the error is from a missing `type="text"` attribute
options.why: They differ: version 2 replaces `size`, while version 1 intersects two incompatible types.

explanation: `ComponentProps<'input'>` includes the native `size?: number`. Intersecting it with `{ size: 'sm' | 'lg' }` leaves no type that satisfies both, so TypeScript reduces the whole props type to `never` ("property 'size' has conflicting types"). Omit the native key before adding your own: `Omit<ComponentProps<'input'>, 'size'> & { size: … }`. Then destructure `size` before spreading the rest onto `<input>`. Verified with TypeScript 6 and @types/react 19.
reference: React TypeScript Cheatsheet: Wrapping native elements

options.text: `<Action as="button" onClick={save} />`, because `onClick` must be optional
options.why: This matches the button variant exactly, so it compiles.

options.text: `function Action({ as, href }: ActionProps)`, because `href` isn't on every variant
options.why: Destructuring before narrowing reads a key that the button variant lacks.

options.text: `props.href` inside the `as === 'link'` branch, because unions can't be narrowed in JSX
options.why: Comparing the discriminant narrows `props`, so `props.href` is fine there.

options.text: `<Action as="link" href="/home" />`, because `href` conflicts with the native `<a>` prop
options.why: This matches the link variant and compiles cleanly.

explanation: A discriminated union makes invalid prop combinations unrepresentable: `<Action as="link" onClick={…} />` is rejected because the link variant has no `onClick`. Narrow on the discriminant before touching variant-only keys. Destructuring `href` in the parameter list reads it before narrowing, which TypeScript rejects ("Property 'href' does not exist on type 'ActionProps'"). Narrowing with `props.as === 'link'` and then reading `props.href` compiles. Verified with TypeScript 6.

options.text: Nothing: `as User` and `safeParse` both check the shape at runtime
options.why: `as` is a compile-time assertion only; it performs no check at all.

options.text: `safeParse` throws a `TypeError` that crashes the request handler
options.why: `safeParse` never throws on bad data; it returns a result object.

options.text: `result.success` is `false` with an `invalid_type` issue at `id`
options.why: With `as`, the string id would flow silently into code expecting a number.

options.text: Zod coerces `"7"` to `7` by default, so `result.data.id` is the number 7
options.why: Plain `z.number()` doesn't coerce; only `z.coerce.number()` does.

explanation: A type assertion such as `as User` only tells the compiler to trust you, so malformed API data reaches the UI unchecked. A schema validates at runtime. `safeParse` returns `{ success: false, error }` (here an `invalid_type` issue at path `id`) or `{ success: true, data }`, and `z.infer<typeof User>` derives the static type from the same schema. Zod also strips unknown keys by default. Verified with Zod 4.6: `{ id: '7' }` failed with `invalid_type` at `id`, and an extra key was dropped from `data`.

options.text: The child path must be absolute: `path="/settings/profile"`
options.why: Relative child paths are the normal way to nest; the route already matches.

options.text: An `<Outlet />` inside `SettingsLayout`, where the matched child renders
options.why: A parent route renders its matching child only where it places `<Outlet />`.

options.text: A `key` on the inner `<Route>` so React can tell the two routes apart
options.why: Keys don't affect route matching or where children render.

options.text: Wrapping `<Profile />` in `<Suspense>`, because nested routes load lazily
options.why: Nothing here is lazy; the child simply has nowhere to render.

explanation: Nested routes compose layouts: when `/settings/profile` matches, React Router renders `SettingsLayout`, and the matched child element appears wherever the parent renders `<Outlet />`. Without an outlet, the child route matches but has nowhere to render. This is the same in React Router v6 and v7.
reference: React Router docs: Nested routes and Outlet

stem: Which two statements about navigation in a React Router app are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: `<Link to="/orders">` navigates on the client without reloading the document
options.why: It pushes a history entry and re-renders the matched routes, so app state survives.

options.text: `useParams()` returns route params as strings, so `/orders/007` gives `{ id: "007" }`
options.why: URL params are always strings (or undefined); convert them yourself.

options.text: `<a href="/orders">` is equivalent to `<Link>`, because React Router intercepts every anchor
options.why: A plain anchor triggers a full document load, losing in-memory state.

options.text: `useNavigate()` returns the current location, and `useLocation()` performs navigation
options.why: It's the other way round: `useNavigate` returns a function that navigates.

options.text: Calling `navigate('/home')` during render is the recommended way to redirect
options.why: Navigate in effects or event handlers, or render `<Navigate>`; not during render.

explanation: `<Link>` does client-side navigation through the History API, so the page isn't reloaded and in-memory state is kept. A plain `<a href>` does a full document load. `useParams()` returns strings (or `undefined`), so `Number(id)` or validation is needed. `useNavigate()` returns an imperative `navigate` function for event handlers and effects, and `useLocation()` reads the current location.

stem: A React Router app has the nested routes `/projects/:id` (layout) and `/projects/:id/tasks` (child). Each component fetches its data in `useEffect`, so the tasks request starts only after the project layout has rendered. What do route loaders (data or framework mode) change?

options.text: Nothing: loaders also run one after another, parent first, child after it renders
options.why: Loaders for all matched routes start together, before rendering.

options.text: Loaders replace `fetch` with a cached client, so repeated visits never refetch
options.why: Loaders are functions you write; they don't add a cache by themselves.

options.text: Both loaders start in parallel before rendering, removing the waterfall
options.why: Components then read their data with `useLoaderData()`.

options.text: Loaders run on the server only, so client-only apps cannot use them
options.why: In data mode they run in the browser too; framework mode adds server loaders.

explanation: Fetching in `useEffect` creates render-then-fetch waterfalls: the child can't start until the parent has rendered. When navigation begins, React Router's loaders run for every matched route in parallel, and the route components render with data already available through `useLoaderData()`. The same idea drives TanStack Router loaders and React Server Components: start data loading as early as possible, outside the render tree.

stem: Why do teams pick TanStack Router over a string-based router for a large TypeScript app?

options.text: It renders on the server only, so pages need no client JavaScript
options.why: It is a client router (with SSR support); it doesn't remove client JavaScript.

options.text: Routes, params and search params are typed, with `validateSearch` parsing
options.why: A typo in `to`, a missing param or a bad search value becomes a compile error.

options.text: It stores route state in Redux automatically, so time-travel debugging works
options.why: TanStack Router has no Redux integration; its state is internal and typed.

options.text: It removes the need for nested layouts by flattening every route to one level
options.why: It supports nested and layout routes, just like React Router.

explanation: TanStack Router builds a typed route tree. `<Link to="/posts/$postId" params={{ postId }}>` is checked against real routes, and `validateSearch` (often with Zod) turns the query string into typed, validated state. Search params can then act as first-class application state, such as filters and pagination, without stringly-typed parsing. It also offers loaders with built-in caching.
reference: TanStack Router docs: Type safety and search params

options.text: CSS Modules only work with Tailwind, so the import is ignored
options.why: CSS Modules work with plain CSS files named `*.module.css`.

options.text: Keys keep their original names, so read `styles['btn-primary']` instead
options.why: Vite doesn't camel-case keys unless `css.modules.localsConvention` is set.

options.text: CSS Modules scope classes to one file, so `.btn-primary` must be marked `:global`
options.why: Local scoping is the point; the generated name is exported for you to use.

options.text: Vite inlines module classes at build time, so they only work in production
options.why: CSS Modules work the same way in dev and production builds.

explanation: A CSS Module turns each class into a unique, hashed name and exports a mapping object. By default Vite exports the original class names unchanged, so a kebab-case class must be read as `styles['btn-primary']`. `styles.btnPrimary` is `undefined`, and React renders no class at all. Set `css.modules.localsConvention: 'camelCaseOnly'` if you prefer camelCase keys. Checked against Vite 8.3, which passes `localsConvention` through unset by default.

options.text: Template literals are not allowed in `className`; it must be a plain string
options.why: Any string expression is valid in `className`; the problem is CSS generation.

options.text: Tailwind only generates classes it finds as complete strings in source
options.why: Map props to full class names, such as `{ red: 'bg-red-500' }[color]`.

options.text: `px-2` overrides the background, because spacing utilities are applied last
options.why: Spacing and background utilities don't conflict.

options.text: React strips unknown classes at runtime unless they appear in the stylesheet
options.why: React passes class strings through unchanged.

explanation: Tailwind scans source files for complete class names and generates CSS only for those it finds. A class assembled at runtime, such as `` `bg-${color}-500` ``, never appears in the source, so no CSS is generated for it. Use complete literal class names, for example from a lookup object (`{ red: 'bg-red-500', blue: 'bg-blue-500' }[color]`), or safelist the classes explicitly.
reference: Tailwind CSS docs: Dynamic class names

stem: A team moves a styled-components app to React Server Components. Why do runtime CSS-in-JS libraries cause trouble there, and what is the usual direction?

options.text: They inject styles at render time via context, so they need Client Components; teams go zero-runtime
options.why: Options include CSS Modules, Tailwind, Panda CSS or vanilla-extract.

options.text: Server Components can't import any CSS at all, so every style must move into inline `style` props
options.why: Server Components can import CSS files and CSS Modules normally.

options.text: They work unchanged; the only cost is slightly larger HTML because styles are inlined by the server
options.why: They rely on context and runtime injection, which Server Components don't support.

options.text: React 19 bans third-party styling libraries, so every component must use the `<style>` tag with `precedence`
options.why: Nothing is banned; React 19 just adds stylesheet support alongside existing approaches.

explanation: Runtime CSS-in-JS libraries such as styled-components and Emotion compute styles in JavaScript while rendering, read themes from React context, and inject `<style>` tags. Server Components have no context or state, so those components must be Client Components. On top of that, style injection during streaming needs framework hooks, and computing styles costs CPU on every render. Build-time approaches avoid all of this: CSS Modules, Tailwind, and zero-runtime CSS-in-JS such as Panda CSS or vanilla-extract.
reference: React docs and Next.js docs: CSS-in-JS

stem: How does shadcn/ui differ from a component library such as MUI that you install from npm?

options.text: It renders components in an iframe so their styles never leak into the app
options.why: Components render normally in your tree; there is no iframe.

options.text: Its components ship precompiled, so you configure them through a theme object only
options.why: That describes a packaged library; shadcn/ui gives you editable source instead.

options.text: Its CLI copies component source (Radix plus Tailwind) into your repo
options.why: Upgrades aren't `npm update`; you pull in changes yourself.

options.text: It only works with Next.js because its components are Server Components
options.why: It works with Vite, Remix and other React setups too.

explanation: shadcn/ui is "a collection of components you copy into your project". `npx shadcn add dialog` writes the component's source into your codebase, usually `components/ui`. It builds on headless primitives such as Radix UI for behaviour and accessibility, and on Tailwind for styling. You get full control and no dependency lock-in, at the cost of maintaining that code yourself. Packaged libraries such as MUI are versioned dependencies that you customise through themes and props.

stem: With Radix UI, what does this render? ```jsx Open help ```

options.text: A `<button>` that wraps the `<a>`, keeping both elements in the DOM
options.why: `asChild` replaces the default `<button>` rather than wrapping the child.

options.text: Only the `<a>`, with Radix props merged in, including `type="button"`
options.why: Radix's Slot merges its props, handlers and ARIA attributes onto your element.

options.text: The `<a>` unchanged; `asChild` hands all trigger behaviour to the child to implement
options.why: The child receives Radix's props and handlers; you don't reimplement them.

options.text: Nothing: `asChild` requires a Radix component as its child, not a plain element
options.why: Any element or component that spreads its props works.

explanation: Headless libraries provide behaviour and accessibility without styles. Radix's `asChild` prop uses a Slot: instead of rendering its default `<button>`, the trigger merges its props onto the single child (`aria-haspopup`, `aria-expanded`, `data-state`, the event handlers, and here also `type="button"`). You choose the element and styles, and Radix supplies the behaviour. Custom components used with `asChild` must spread incoming props and forward the ref. Verified by server-rendering Radix Dialog 1.1 with React 19.3.

stem: A team must choose between a styled component library (MUI, Chakra UI) and headless primitives (Radix UI, React Aria). Which statement best captures the trade-off?

options.text: Styled libraries are always inaccessible, so headless primitives are the only accessible option
options.why: Mature styled libraries also handle accessibility; that isn't the trade-off.

options.text: Styled kits give a design system fast; headless ones give behaviour while you style
options.why: Pick by how custom the design must be and how much styling work you want.

options.text: Headless libraries are Server Components only, while styled libraries are client-only
options.why: Interactive primitives in both kinds run as Client Components.

options.text: Headless primitives can't be themed, so a design system must be built on a styled library
options.why: Headless primitives are unstyled precisely so you can style them any way.

explanation: Styled kits such as MUI and Chakra ship a complete look, theming and many components, which suits teams that accept or lightly adapt that design. Headless primitives such as Radix UI, React Aria and Ark UI implement the hard parts (focus management, keyboard support, ARIA, positioning) and render unstyled, so a bespoke design system can be built on top, often with Tailwind. The cost is more styling work. shadcn/ui sits in between, offering styled starting points on headless primitives.
reference: React Aria docs: Introduction; Radix UI docs

stem:
With Motion (formerly Framer Motion), the panel fades in but disappears instantly when `open` becomes false; the `exit` animation never plays. What is wrong?

```jsx
{open && (
  <motion.div key="panel" initial={{ opacity: 0 }} animate={{ opacity: 1 }} exit={{ opacity: 0 }}>
    Settings
  </motion.div>
)}
```

options.text: `exit` only works when the `motion` element is the direct child of `AnimatePresence`
options.why: A nested `motion` element inside a keyed child also runs its exit animation.

options.text: It isn't wrapped in `<AnimatePresence>`, so React unmounts it at once
options.why: `AnimatePresence` keeps removed children mounted until their exit animation finishes.

options.text: `exit` needs a `transition` with a duration, or it completes in zero frames
options.why: A default transition applies; the element is removed before any animation starts.

options.text: Opacity can't be animated on unmount; only transform properties support `exit`
options.why: Opacity is a standard exit target; the problem is unmounting.

explanation: React unmounts an element as soon as its condition becomes false, so nothing remains to animate. `AnimatePresence` detects children leaving the tree and keeps them rendered until their `exit` animations finish. Its direct children need stable keys. Verified with Motion 13.4 in jsdom: without `AnimatePresence` the element vanished right after the toggle. With it, the element was still present and was removed after the transition, including when the `motion.div` sat inside a wrapper component.

stem: A drawer slides in by animating `left` from `-300px` to `0`, and it stutters on mid-range phones. Which change helps most?

options.text: Animate `transform: translateX()` and `opacity`, which the compositor can run
options.why: Changing `left` re-runs layout and paint on every frame; transforms usually don't.

options.text: Wrap the drawer in `React.memo` so it doesn't re-render while it animates
options.why: The cost is browser layout and paint per frame, not React renders.

options.text: Animate `width` from 0 to 300px instead, because width is cheaper than position
options.why: Width also triggers layout on every frame, and often affects siblings too.

options.text: Increase the animation duration so the browser has more time per frame
options.why: Longer animations still need 60 fps; each frame stays just as expensive.

explanation: Properties like `left`, `top` and `width` force layout and paint on each frame. `transform` and `opacity` can usually be animated by the compositor, which keeps animations smooth even while the main thread is busy. Libraries such as Motion animate transforms for exactly this reason. Also respect users who prefer less motion: honour `prefers-reduced-motion`, for example with Motion's `useReducedMotion()`.

stem: Match each animation tool with the model it is built around.

options.text: Declarative props on components, with `exit` and `layout` animations
Physics-based springs driven by mass, tension and friction
Imperative timelines and tweens that work in any framework
Browser-native transitions defined entirely in stylesheets

explanation: Motion animates by props (`animate`, `exit`, `layout`) and integrates with React's lifecycle through `AnimatePresence`. react-spring models motion as springs instead of fixed durations, so animations feel physical and can be interrupted smoothly. GSAP (GreenSock) is an imperative, framework-agnostic engine with powerful timelines; in React it is used through refs and the `useGSAP` hook. Plain CSS transitions and keyframes need no JavaScript and suit simple state changes.

stem: A component starts a GSAP timeline in `useEffect` without returning a cleanup. In development with StrictMode, the intro animation plays twice and stray tweens keep running after navigation. What is the recommended fix?

options.text: Switch to `useLayoutEffect`, because GSAP animations must run before paint
options.why: The timing isn't the problem; the missing cleanup is.

options.text: Disable StrictMode, since the double run only happens in development
options.why: The leak on unmount happens in production too; StrictMode just exposes it.

options.text: Use `useGSAP()` or `gsap.context()`, so cleanup reverts the tweens
options.why: Reverting kills the tweens and restores inline styles when the effect is cleaned up.

options.text: Store the timeline in state so React keeps one instance between renders
options.why: State doesn't clean up running tweens and adds needless re-renders.

explanation: Imperative animation libraries create work that React doesn't know about, so each effect must undo it. GSAP's `useGSAP()` hook from `@gsap/react` wraps your code in a `gsap.context()` and calls `revert()` automatically on unmount: tweens are killed and inline styles restored. That makes StrictMode's mount, unmount and remount cycle harmless and stops tweens leaking after navigation.

stem: A Vite + React project is choosing a unit test runner. Why do many teams pick Vitest over Jest here?

options.text: Vitest runs tests in real browsers only, so jsdom is never needed
options.why: Vitest runs in Node with jsdom or happy-dom by default; browser mode is optional.

options.text: It reuses Vite's config and transforms, supports ESM and TS, mirrors Jest
options.why: Aliases and plugins work in tests without a separate Babel or ts-jest setup.

options.text: Jest can't test React components at all, so Vitest is required for Testing Library
options.why: Jest works with React Testing Library; it just needs its own transform setup.

options.text: Vitest skips type checking, so tests always run faster than with any other runner
options.why: Neither runner type-checks by default; the gain comes from sharing Vite's pipeline.

explanation: Vitest is built on Vite. It reads `vite.config`, reuses its plugins and aliases, transforms TypeScript and JSX with the same pipeline, supports ESM natively, and exposes `describe`, `it`, `expect` and `vi.fn()` with Jest-compatible semantics. Jest uses its own transform system (Babel or ts-jest) and treats ESM as experimental, so a Vite app needs duplicate configuration. Both work with React Testing Library.

stem: A "Show details" panel is hidden with a CSS class from a stylesheet. A React Testing Library test in jsdom passes, but in Chrome the panel never appears. Which test catches this bug, and why?

options.text: Playwright, because a real browser applies the CSS that hides the details panel
options.why: jsdom doesn't load or apply stylesheets, so visibility from CSS goes unchecked.

options.text: A snapshot test, because snapshots include the computed styles of every element
options.why: DOM snapshots record markup, not computed styles from stylesheets.

options.text: The same RTL test with `toBeVisible()`, because jsdom applies all imported stylesheets
options.why: jsdom ignores stylesheets, so `toBeVisible()` can't see class-based hiding.

options.text: A test that uses `fireEvent.click` instead of `userEvent.click`, because it is closer to the browser
options.why: Both run in jsdom without CSS; the event API isn't the gap.

explanation: jsdom implements the DOM but not layout or stylesheet application, so class-based visibility, overlapping elements and responsive breakpoints are invisible to component tests. End-to-end tools such as Playwright or Cypress run a real browser engine. Playwright's locators auto-wait, and its web-first assertions like `await expect(page.getByText('Details')).toBeVisible()` retry until the condition holds. Keep many fast component tests and a few E2E tests on critical flows.
reference: Playwright docs: Assertions; Testing Library docs: jsdom limitations

stem: Which two statements about Playwright and Cypress are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: Playwright drives Chromium, Firefox and WebKit through one API, from outside the browser
options.why: It controls browsers over a protocol, so multiple tabs and origins are easy.

options.text: Cypress commands are queued and retried, not promises you can `await` directly
options.why: Write `cy.get('.item').should('have.length', 3)` instead of awaiting results.

options.text: Both tools run tests inside jsdom, so neither needs a real browser installed
options.why: Both drive real browsers; that is why they catch CSS and layout bugs.

options.text: Playwright can't test anything that opens a second tab or window
options.why: Multiple pages and contexts are a core Playwright feature.

options.text: Cypress tests run in Node.js and talk to the browser only through HTTP requests
options.why: Cypress runs test code inside the browser, next to the application.

explanation: Playwright runs tests in Node.js and controls Chromium, Firefox and WebKit over a protocol, which makes multiple tabs, origins and browser contexts straightforward. Cypress runs your test code inside the browser alongside the app. Its commands are added to a queue and retried until assertions pass, which gives readable chained tests but means you can't `await` a command's value. Both auto-wait for elements and catch real-browser bugs that jsdom misses.
reference: Playwright docs; Cypress docs: Introduction to Cypress

stem: A component loads data with `fetch('/api/orders').then(r => r.json()).then(setOrders).catch(showError)`. When the API returns 404 with an HTML error page, what happens, and how does axios differ?

options.text: `fetch` rejects on any non-2xx status, so `showError` runs, just like axios
options.why: `fetch` rejects only on network failures; HTTP errors still resolve.

options.text: `fetch` resolves, so `r.json()` fails on HTML; axios rejects a 404
options.why: With `fetch`, check `res.ok` (or `res.status`) before parsing.

options.text: Both resolve normally and pass the error page to `setOrders` as a string
options.why: Here `r.json()` throws on HTML; and axios rejects non-2xx responses by default.

options.text: `fetch` retries 404s three times automatically before resolving
options.why: `fetch` never retries; retries come from libraries or your own code.

explanation: The `fetch` promise rejects only when the request can't be completed, such as a network error or an abort. A 404 or 500 still resolves with `res.ok === false`. Here `r.json()` then throws a parse error on the HTML, so the user sees a confusing message rather than "not found". Check `if (!res.ok) throw new Error(…)`. axios rejects for statuses outside 2xx by default (`validateStatus`), parses JSON for you, and also supports `AbortController` signals for cancellation.
reference: MDN: Using Fetch; axios docs: Handling errors

stem:
With SWR, a profile panel should load only once a user is selected. Which code does that correctly?

```jsx
const { data } = useSWR(/* ? */, fetcher);
```

options.text: `` `/api/users/${selectedId}` ``, because SWR skips URLs that contain `undefined`
options.why: SWR would request `/api/users/undefined`; it doesn't inspect the URL.

options.text: `selectedId ? '/api/users/' + selectedId : null`; a `null` key skips fetching
options.why: When the key becomes a string, SWR fetches, and identical keys share one request.

options.text: Call `useSWR` inside `if (selectedId) { … }`, so the hook runs only when needed
options.why: Hooks can't be called conditionally; use a conditional key instead.

options.text: Pass `{ enabled: Boolean(selectedId) }` as the third argument, as in TanStack Query
options.why: That option belongs to TanStack Query; SWR uses a falsy key for this.

explanation: SWR (stale-while-revalidate) identifies data by its key. When the key is `null` or falsy, or a function that returns one, SWR doesn't start a request, which is how you express dependent fetching without breaking the rules of hooks. Once a key is set, components using the same key share one cached request (deduplicated) and revalidate on focus and reconnect by default.

stem: An RTK Query API defines `getPosts` with `providesTags: ['Post']` and `addPost` with `invalidatesTags: ['Post']`. After `addPost` succeeds, what happens to a mounted list that uses `useGetPostsQuery()`?

options.text: Nothing until the user reloads, because RTK Query caches forever by default
options.why: Tag invalidation exists precisely to refetch stale cached data.

options.text: It refetches `getPosts`, whose cached result provides the invalidated tag
options.why: Subscribed queries with a matching tag refetch automatically.

options.text: The new post is inserted locally from the mutation's request body, with no refetch
options.why: That is an optimistic or manual cache update, which you must write yourself.

options.text: Every query in the API refetches, because any mutation clears the whole cache
options.why: Only queries whose tags match the invalidated tags are refetched.

explanation: RTK Query links queries and mutations through tags. Queries declare what they provide (`providesTags`), and mutations declare what they make stale (`invalidatesTags`). When a mutation completes, matching cached entries are marked invalid, and any query still subscribed refetches. Use tags with IDs, such as `{ type: 'Post', id }`, for finer control, or `onQueryStarted` for optimistic updates.
reference: Redux Toolkit docs: RTK Query automated re-fetching

stem: An app uses Apollo Client's normalised cache. The `RenameTodo` mutation returns `{ id, title }` for the edited todo, and `AddTodo` returns `{ id, title }` for a new one. Which describes what updates automatically?

options.text: Both: Apollo refetches every active query after any mutation completes
options.why: Apollo doesn't refetch everything; it merges mutation results into the cache.

options.text: Neither: a normalised cache never updates from mutation results, only from queries
options.why: Mutation results are written into the normalised cache like query results.

options.text: The rename shows everywhere; the new todo needs a cache update or refetch
options.why: The cache merges entities by `__typename` and `id`, but can't know which lists gain the new item.

options.text: The new todo appears in every list, but the rename needs `refetchQueries` because titles aren't cached
options.why: It's the reverse: edits to known entities merge automatically, while list membership does not.

explanation: Normalised GraphQL caches (Apollo InMemoryCache, urql Graphcache, Relay) store each object once under a key such as `Todo:42`. When a mutation returns that object's `id` and changed fields, every query that references it re-renders with the new title. A brand-new object isn't part of any cached list, so you add it with `cache.modify`/`update`, `refetchQueries`, or Relay's connection updaters. urql's default document cache is not normalised and instead invalidates queries by `__typename`.
reference: Apollo Client docs: Caching (normalisation) and mutations

options.text: MobX state must be copied immutably, like React state, before React notices changes
options.why: MobX is built on mutation; observables are meant to be changed in place.

options.text: It isn't wrapped in `observer()`, so it tracks no observables it reads
options.why: `observer` subscribes a component to exactly the observables it used while rendering.

options.text: `store.items` must be passed as a prop, because MobX ignores module-level stores
options.why: Stores can be imported directly; what matters is observation.

options.text: MobX only works with class components, so `TodoList` must be converted
options.why: `mobx-react-lite`'s `observer` is designed for function components.

explanation: MobX makes state observable and lets you mutate it directly, as in `store.items.push(todo)`. Components re-render only if they are reactive: `observer(TodoList)` records which observables were read during render and re-renders when any of them change, which gives fine-grained updates without selectors. A plain function component isn't subscribed, so mutations go unnoticed. Making changes inside actions also batches them.

stem: How does Formik manage form data, and what does that imply compared with React Hook Form?

options.text: Formik reads values from the DOM only on submit, so it never re-renders while typing
options.why: That describes React Hook Form's uncontrolled approach, not Formik.

options.text: Formik keeps values in React state, so typing re-renders the form
options.why: This is simple to reason about, but large forms re-render more.

options.text: Formik can only validate on submit, because it has no field-level validation
options.why: It validates on change, blur or submit, and supports field-level validators.

options.text: Formik requires Redux to store form state across components
options.why: Formik keeps form state in its own React state and context.

explanation: Formik keeps `values`, `errors` and `touched` in React state, and `<Field>`/`getFieldProps` wire inputs as controlled components. Each keystroke updates state, so the form (or its fields) re-render, which is fine for small forms but costly for very large ones. Validation can use a `validate` function or a Yup `validationSchema`. React Hook Form instead registers uncontrolled inputs and reads values through refs, so typing usually doesn't re-render the form.

options.text: `<Image source={logo} />`, because images must be wrapped in `<Text>` to render
options.why: `Image` is a native component that can sit directly inside a `View`.

options.text: `Hello, {name}`, because raw text can't sit directly inside a `<View>`
options.why: React Native renders native views, and only `<Text>` can display strings.

options.text: `<Text>Welcome back</Text>`, because `Text` can't be a child of `View`
options.why: Putting `Text` inside `View` is the normal pattern.

options.text: `style={styles.box}`, because React Native requires `className` for styling
options.why: React Native has no CSS classes; `style` objects are the standard approach.

explanation: React Native renders to native platform views, not the DOM. There are no `<div>` or `<span>` elements, no cascading stylesheets, and text is special: every string must live inside a `<Text>` component. Layout uses Flexbox with `flexDirection: 'column'` by default. The React model of components, props, state and hooks carries over unchanged, which is why web React skills transfer.

stem: A React Native screen renders 5,000 messages with `<ScrollView>{messages.map(m => <Message key={m.id} {...m} />)}</ScrollView>`. Scrolling janks and memory is high. What is the standard fix?

options.text: Wrap `Message` in `React.memo`, since the cost comes from re-rendering unchanged rows
options.why: All 5,000 rows are mounted at once; memo doesn't reduce that.

options.text: Use `FlatList` (or FlashList), which renders only rows near the viewport
options.why: Pass `data`, `renderItem` and `keyExtractor`; offscreen rows aren't mounted.

options.text: Move the list into a Web Worker so rendering runs off the UI thread
options.why: Native views must be created on the UI side; workers can't render components.

options.text: Set `removeClippedSubviews={false}` so React Native keeps every row ready
options.why: That keeps more views alive, which makes memory use worse.

explanation: `ScrollView` renders all of its children up front. `FlatList` virtualises: it renders a window of items around the viewport and recycles as you scroll, keeping memory and mount time bounded. Tune it with `keyExtractor`, `getItemLayout` for fixed-height rows, `initialNumToRender` and `windowSize`, or use Shopify's FlashList for heavier lists. This is the native equivalent of list virtualisation on the web with libraries like react-window.
reference: React Native docs: FlatList and optimising lists

stem: In a Vite + React app, `.env` contains `API_URL=https://api.example.com` and `VITE_API_URL=https://api.example.com`. Which expression gives the URL in browser code?

options.text: `process.env.API_URL`, the standard Node way to read environment variables
options.why: `process.env` doesn't exist in browser code built by Vite.

options.text: `import.meta.env.API_URL`, since Vite exposes every `.env` key to the client
options.why: Only keys with the `VITE_` prefix are exposed, which protects secrets.

options.text: `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL`, because only `VITE_` keys reach the client
options.why: Never put secrets in `VITE_` variables: they are inlined into the bundle.

options.text: `window.env.VITE_API_URL`, which Vite injects into `index.html` at runtime
options.why: Vite replaces `import.meta.env` values at build time; there is no `window.env`.

explanation: Vite exposes environment variables through `import.meta.env`, but only those starting with `envPrefix` (default `VITE_`). They are statically replaced in the client bundle at build time. Unprefixed variables such as `API_URL` stay private to config and server code, which keeps secrets out of the browser. Anything with the prefix is public once bundled. Checked against Vite 8.3, whose default `envPrefix` is `"VITE_"`.
reference: Vite docs: Env variables and modes

options.text: Fast Refresh needs files that export only components, and `MAX` breaks that
options.why: Move `MAX` to its own module so `Counter.jsx` exports only components.

options.text: Components with `useState` can never be hot-updated, so any edit resets state
options.why: Fast Refresh exists precisely to keep hook state across edits.

options.text: Vite's dev server bundles the whole app on each change, so every edit is a full reload
options.why: Vite serves native ES modules and updates only what changed.

options.text: Named exports aren't supported by Fast Refresh; components must be `export default`
options.why: Named component exports work fine with Fast Refresh.

explanation: React Fast Refresh, used by `@vitejs/plugin-react`, can swap a module in place and keep component state only when the module exports React components alone. Exporting a constant, a helper or a context from the same file means the module can't be safely hot-replaced, so the update falls back to re-running its importers or reloading the page, and state is lost. The `react-refresh/only-export-components` ESLint rule flags these files. Also note that Vite serves native ESM in development, pre-bundles dependencies, and in Vite 8 builds with Rolldown.

stem: An Astro page renders a React counter as `<Counter />` in a `.astro` file. The count shows `0`, but clicking does nothing. Why?

options.text: Astro only supports Preact, so React components render as plain text
options.why: Astro supports React through its official integration.

options.text: With no `client:*` directive, Astro ships it as static HTML with no JS
options.why: Add `client:load`, `client:idle` or `client:visible` to hydrate this island.

options.text: React components in Astro must be Server Components, so `useState` is ignored
options.why: Hydrated islands run as normal client React; the component just isn't hydrated.

options.text: The click handler needs `onclick` in lowercase, as in HTML
options.why: No handler runs because no JavaScript is shipped, whatever the casing.

explanation: Astro uses an islands architecture. Framework components render to HTML on the server by default, with zero client JavaScript. Interactivity is opt-in per component: `client:load` hydrates immediately, `client:idle` waits until the browser is idle, `client:visible` waits until it scrolls into view, and `client:only="react"` skips server rendering. That makes content-heavy sites fast, but a component without a directive is static HTML.

stem: A `MouseTracker` component exposes the pointer position through a render prop, as in `<MouseTracker render={({ x, y }) => <Cursor x={x} y={y} />} />`. A team refactors it into a `useMousePosition()` custom hook. Which statement about the change is correct?

options.text: The hook version shares one position state between every component that calls it
options.why: Each call to a custom hook gets its own state, just like a render-prop instance.

options.text: Render props are now invalid in React 19, so the refactor is required
options.why: Render props still work; they are just less common since hooks.

options.text: The hook shares the same logic without a wrapper component or function prop
options.why: Hooks replaced most render-prop uses; render props remain handy for render customisation.

options.text: The hook version can't subscribe to window events, because only components can add listeners
options.why: Hooks add and remove listeners in `useEffect` just fine.

explanation: Render props and higher-order components were the main ways to share stateful logic before hooks, and both add wrapper components to the tree. A custom hook shares the logic directly: `const { x, y } = useMousePosition()`. Every caller still gets independent state. Render props remain useful when a component wants callers to control what it renders, for example a list rendering each row through `renderItem`.
reference: React docs: Reusing logic with custom hooks
